WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.TITLE: Security posture & authorized testing scope
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.SUBTITLE: Legitimate security practice only: harden your PatTool deployment, learn defensive basics, and document written authorization before any assessment.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.DISCLAIMER_BODY: PatTool does not scan arbitrary websites or attack servers. Use authorized tooling only on systems you own or where you have explicit written permission. Unauthorized testing is illegal.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.PATTOOL_INTRO: Use this checklist as you operate your own PatTool stack (Spring Boot API + Angular + Keycloak + MongoDB).
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.PATTOOL_ARCH_1: Review Spring Security and JWT rules (SecurityConfig.java): keep defaults restrictive and prefer authenticated APIs.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.PATTOOL_ARCH_2: Protect Keycloak: strong passwords, HTTPS in production, minimal realm/client roles, rotate secrets.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.PATTOOL_ARCH_3: MongoDB: authentication enabled, network isolation, backups encrypted at rest where possible.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.PATTOOL_ARCH_4: Secrets stay out of git: copy application.properties.example → application.properties locally; never commit credentials.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.PATTOOL_ARCH_5: Frontend environment files must point to trusted API and auth endpoints only.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.PATTOOL_OPS_1: Apply OS and JVM patches regularly; restart during maintenance windows.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.PATTOOL_OPS_2: Run dependency scans (e.g. mvn dependency-check, npm audit) and upgrade risky libraries.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.PATTOOL_OPS_3: Keep TLS certificates valid; enable HSTS only where HTTPS is correctly terminated.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.PATTOOL_OPS_4: Centralize logs and monitor auth failures, upload anomalies, and disk usage.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.PATTOOL_OPS_5: Exercise restore drills from Mongo/file backups at least yearly.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.EDU_INTRO: Modern applications face predictable classes of flaws (injection, broken access control, misconfiguration). Understanding them helps you defend rather than attack.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.EDU_RESP_1: If you discover a vulnerability in someone else's system, contact their security team or use their published disclosure policy.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.EDU_RESP_2: Do not access, modify, or exfiltrate data beyond what is necessary to demonstrate impact.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.EDU_RESP_3: Allow reasonable time for remediation before any public discussion.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.EDU_LEGAL: Laws such as the CFAA (US), Computer Misuse Act (UK), and similar statutes elsewhere prohibit unauthorized access regardless of intent.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.SCOPE_INTRO: Record scope before commissioning tests. Buttons below appear only when your administrator configures optional URLs on the server.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.SCOPE_FETCH_ERROR: Could not load server links (sign in and ensure the API is reachable). You can still fill and copy the manifest locally.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.SCOPE_DOMAINS_HINT: One entry per line. Restrict to staging mirrors when possible.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.SCOPE_CONFIRM: I confirm written authorization exists for the listed targets within the stated period.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.COPY_FAIL: Could not copy — confirm the checkbox or retry.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.SCOPE_STORAGE_NOTE: This form is not stored by PatTool; copy the manifest into your ticket system or vault.
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.MANIFEST_FOOTER: Signer acknowledgement captured outside PatTool (ticket reference, PDF mandate, etc.).
WORLD_SECURITY_SCAN.PROBE_INTRO: Runs non-intrusive checks from the PatTool server (headers, HTTPS, certificates, security.txt). Optionally enable active checks: OPTIONS (Allow), TRACE probe, and /robots.txt — still bounded and authorization-required; not penetration testing. LAN targets may need pat.passive-probe.allow-private-targets=true.

UNIVERS_FUTUR.TITLE: Future universe
UNIVERS_FUTUR.SUBTITLE: True positions (no light-travel delay) of planets, stars, constellations and galaxies in X thousand, million or billion years. In the observed model, expansion never ends: everything does not fall back to a point.
UNIVERS_FUTUR.SCENARIO_HINT: ΛCDM: dark energy, accelerated expansion forever. Big Crunch: closed universe with no dark energy, recollapse to a point — not supported by current measurements.
UNIVERS_FUTUR.HINT_SKY: 3D proper motions (Hipparcos): constellations warp. Dim lines = today, bright lines = chosen date. Most realistic up to ~100,000 years.
UNIVERS_FUTUR.HINT_PLANETS: Gravity-bound orbits: the solar system does not expand with the universe. After ~5 Gyr the Sun is a red giant (inner planets leave the model).
UNIVERS_FUTUR.HINT_GALAXIES: Bound Local Group (Andromeda approaches, collision ~4.5 Gyr). Other galaxies follow expansion: proper distance = d₀ × a(t), with no light delay.
UNIVERS_FUTUR.HINT_COSMOS: Bound dots at the centre = Local Group (fixed size). Others recede with a(t). Bottom curve: scale factor. In ΛCDM it never turns down.
UNIVERS_FUTUR.VERDICT_LCDM_BODY: With measured dark energy, a(t) grows without limit. Bound structures (atoms, planets, galaxies) stay bound; distant galaxies recede forever. Nothing returns to a point.
UNIVERS_FUTUR.VERDICT_CRUNCH_BODY: With no dark energy and enough matter, expansion stops then everything falls back to a point (Big Crunch). That is not the observed model — use the slider to see what it would look like.
UNIVERS_FUTUR.VERDICT_CRUNCH_NOW: Everything has returned to a point
UNIVERS_FUTUR.VERDICT_CRUNCH_NOW_BODY: In this hypothetical scenario the scale factor has fallen back to zero: the universe has recollapsed.

EUROMILLIONS.METHOD_CHI2_GOF_UNIFORM_AI_SPEC: BINDING METHOD (user choice: χ² naïve uniform). Scope = JSON `sinceInclusive` / `tail` / `periods` only. (1) Main balls 1–50: let n = number of draws in scope, total slots = 5n. For each k∈{1,…,50}, count O_k = appearances of k across all five positions of all draws (order within a draw irrelevant). Expected E = 5n/50 each. Pearson χ²_main = Σ_k (O_k−E)²/E with df = 49. Use PatTool pre-counts in `periods[].mf` / `chi2MainNaive` as cross-check but recompute from `tail` if you show detail. (2) Stars by FDJ era: assign each draw to period P1/P2/P3 using `periodCuts` and JSON `periods[]` starMax (9 / 11 / 12). Within period j with n_j draws and starMax S_j, pool 2n_j star-slots; counts O_s for s∈{1,…,S_j}; expected E_j = 2n_j/S_j each; χ²_stars,j = Σ_s (O_s−E_j)²/E_j with df = S_j−1. State hypotheses explicitly (uniform marginal over slots within era). Do not replace this by generic multinomial-without-replacement theory unless clearly labeled extra; primary deliverable = these χ² statistics + df + plain interpretation.
EUROMILLIONS.METHOD_ENTROPY_NORMALIZED_AI_SPEC: BINDING METHOD (user choice: normalized Shannon entropy). Scope = draws in `tail` aligned with `periods`. Natural log. (1) Mains: empirical p_k = (count of ball k in pooled 5n slots)/(5n), k=1..50. H_main = −Σ p_k ln p_k (0 ln 0 = 0). H_norm_main = H_main / ln(50) ∈ [0,1]; equals 1 iff uniform on categories. (2) Stars per era j: categories 1..S_j, total slots 2n_j, same formula H_j; H_norm_j = H_j / ln(S_j). Report numeric H and H_norm; interpret as deviation from max-entropy baseline; optional comparison to uniform benchmark.
EUROMILLIONS.METHOD_GAP_RECURRENCE_AI_SPEC: BINDING METHOD (user choice: inter-draw recurrence gaps). Index draws in chronological order as `tail` (index t=0..n−1). For each ball b∈{1,…,50}, list indices T_b where b appears (≤1 per draw). If |T_b|≥2, gaps Δ_i = T_b[i]−T_b[i−1]; mean gap ḡ_b = mean(Δ). Summarize over balls with ≥2 appearances: e.g. mean of ḡ_b, spread (sd/min/max). Descriptive only; links to renewal/inter-arrival intuition allowed but no forecast claim. Ignore balls with <2 hits for ḡ_b.
EUROMILLIONS.METHOD_SUM_CORRELATION_AI_SPEC: BINDING METHOD (user choice: Pearson correlation of sums). Consider draws where there are exactly five main integers in [1,50] and two star integers in [1,starMax] for that draw’s regulatory era (derive starMax from date vs `periodCuts`). Let X = sum of five mains, Y = sum of two stars. Pearson r between X and Y across all qualifying draws; report sample size n_used. State formula r = cov(X,Y)/(σ_X σ_Y). No causal interpretation; mention linear association only.
EUROMILLIONS.METHOD_MONTE_CARLO_MAXFREQ_AI_SPEC: BINDING METHOD (user choice: Monte Carlo calibration of max pooled frequency). From `tail`, pooled main counts over 5n slots; M_obs = max_{k=1..50} count(k). Null operational model for simulation: independent draws, each draw picks 5 distinct mains uniformly from {1,…,50} without replacement across draws’ sampling mechanism is approximated by repeating n independent such draws; replicate R≥800 times; each replicate yields M_sim; empirical one-sided p-value = (#(M_sim ≥ M_obs)+1)/(R+1). State R and that procedure; if you vary R, say so. Not a proof of bias—interpret as descriptive Monte Carlo tail probability.

ABOUT.TITLE: About PatTool
ABOUT.SUBTITLE: Full-stack platform for sportive events, friends, tools, IoT, the sky and the world — designed and built end to end.
ABOUT.INTRO: PatTool is a private social network for organizing sportive activities, with discussions, photo wall, calendar, AI assistant, geo tools, sky finder, compass, Wikipedia, media watchers and home automation.
ABOUT.FEATURES_DESC: Jump to a module. Everything below is available from the application menus.
ABOUT.FEAT_GLOBE: 3D Earth, live ISS, look-up compass, alerts and flights
ABOUT.FEAT_FUTURE_UNIVERSE: True positions (no light delay) in X thousand to billion years; observed expansion has no end
ABOUT.FEAT_ASTRO: Camera finder: planets, stars, galaxies, ISS, Astra 19.2°E, Starlink train; auto-detect; last target saved; Wikipedia card
ABOUT.FEAT_COMPASS: True-north compass, figure-8 calibration and phone sensors
ABOUT.FEAT_DIRECTION: 7-pose camera calibration (azimuth + elevation) for the finder
ABOUT.FEAT_RELIEF: DEM mountain silhouette with vertical OSM peak names (optional rear camera)
ABOUT.FEAT_WIKI: Wikipedia search: summary, image and article link
ABOUT.SPRING_BOOT_DESC: Spring Boot with Security, WebSocket, MongoDB and OpenAPI
ABOUT.API_DESC: RESTful API with OpenAPI / Swagger documentation
ABOUT.MONGODB_DESC: Cloud NoSQL document database with authentication
ABOUT.DISCUSSION_DESC: Real-time discussion via WebSocket (STOMP/SockJS) with backend persistence (Spring Boot).
ABOUT.SPRING_SECURITY_DESC: Spring Security with JWT / OAuth2 resource server
ABOUT.SSL_DESC: Secure communication with TLS certificates in production
ABOUT.RESOURCES_DESC: Documentation, administration consoles and repositories used by this deployment.
ABOUT.STREAMING_ARCHITECTURE_DESC: Hybrid streaming system with client-side caching
ABOUT.STREAMING_OVERVIEW: The system uses a hybrid approach: backend streams ALL events once via Server-Sent Events (SSE), frontend caches ALL events in memory, and displays only 8 at a time with client-side pagination.
ABOUT.STREAMING_BACKEND_DESC: Backend streams all matching events from MongoDB via SSE, one by one, in real-time.
ABOUT.STREAMING_FRONTEND_DESC: Frontend caches all events in memory. Scrolling uses cached data — no backend calls.
ABOUT.STREAMING_BENEFITS_DESC: Fast scrolling with no network latency, instant display of next pages, offline-ready, instant search/filter on cached data.
ABOUT.STREAMING_APPROACH_DESC: Stream once, cache all, client-side pagination

ASTRO_COMPASS.TITLE: Sky finder
ASTRO_COMPASS.VISIBLE_ONLY_HINT: Show only targets currently above the horizon from your position.
ASTRO_COMPASS.TICKER_ENABLED_HINT: Show a scrolling ticker (like the globe) with the selected object’s details.

ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_AZIMUTH_DEF: Horizontal angle from true North, clockwise. 0° = North, 90° = East, 180° = South, 270° = West. This is the direction to turn to aim at the object.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ELEVATION_DEF: Vertical angle above the horizon. 0° = horizon, 90° = zenith (straight overhead). A negative value means the object is below the horizon, so it is not visible.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_HORIZON_DEF: The line where sky meets ground (elevation 0°). An object “above the horizon” is visible; “below the horizon” is hidden by Earth.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_HEADING_DEF: Direction the top (or camera) of the phone is pointing, relative to North. Compare it with the target azimuth to know whether to turn left or right.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_HUD_TARGET_DEF: Direction and elevation of the object you selected (Sun, ISS, star…). These values do not change when you turn the phone: that is where to aim.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_HUD_CAMERA_DEF: Current direction and elevation of the rear camera. The large numbers follow the phone. The arrows show how far to turn or tilt to reach the target.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_RA_DEF: Celestial equivalent of longitude, given in hours (0–24 h). Together with declination, it fixes an object on the celestial sphere, independent of your location.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_DEC_DEF: Celestial equivalent of latitude. From −90° (south celestial pole) to +90° (north celestial pole). 0° = celestial equator.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_MAG_DEF: Apparent brightness scale: the smaller the number (even negative), the brighter the object. Sirius ≈ −1.5; a star barely visible to the naked eye ≈ +6.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_PHASE_DEF: Portion of the body lit by the Sun as seen from Earth (0% = new Moon, 100% = full Moon). Mainly used for the Moon and inner planets.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_PHASE_ANGLE_DEF: Sun–object–Earth angle. 0° = fully lit (opposition), near 180° = almost fully dark (conjunction).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ELONG_DEF: Apparent angular distance between the object and the Sun, as seen from Earth. Useful for Mercury and Venus: a large elongation places them farther from the Sun in the sky.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_GEO_DEF: Distance from you to the object: light-travel time, astronomical units (AU), and kilometres.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_HELIO_DEF: Distance from the object to the Sun, in AU and kilometres. It changes along the orbit (perihelion / aphelion).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_AU_DEF: Mean Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km. Used for distances in the Solar System.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_CONST_DEF: Sky region where the object lies, among the 88 official constellations. It is a sky map division, not a physical group of stars.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_RISE_DEF: Time when the object crosses from below to above the horizon (elevation 0° going up). For a satellite, this is the start of the pass.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SET_DEF: Time when the object goes back below the horizon. For a satellite, this is the end of the pass.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_CULM_DEF: Time when the object reaches its highest elevation in the sky from your location. Often the best moment to observe it.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_TRANSIT_DEF: Time when the object crosses the local meridian (the North–South line through the zenith). Usually coincides with culmination.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_CIRCUM_DEF: An object that never sets at your latitude: it stays above the horizon (e.g. Polaris in France).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_VISWIN_DEF: How long the object stays above the horizon, from rise to set (or during a satellite pass).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ALT_DEF: Height of the satellite above Earth’s surface, in km. Do not confuse it with elevation, which is the angle in the sky.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SLANT_DEF: Straight-line distance from you to the satellite, longer than the ground distance because it includes altitude.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_GROUND_DEF: Distance along Earth between your position and the ground point directly under the satellite (nadir).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_PASS_DEF: Interval while a satellite is above the horizon from your location. The higher the pass, the easier it is to see.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_VEL_DEF: Orbital speed of the satellite. The ISS travels about 27,600 km/h and crosses the sky in a few minutes.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LAT_DEF: North–south position on Earth (−90° to +90°). It decides which objects are circumpolar and how high they can rise.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LON_DEF: East–west position on Earth (−180° to +180°). With latitude and time, it sets an object’s azimuth and elevation.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_PITCH_DEF: Angle of the top of the phone: 0° = flat (screen to the sky), 90° = vertical. To aim at an object, tilt should match its elevation.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_TRUE_N_DEF: True North points to Earth’s geographic North Pole. Magnetic North follows the magnetic field and is offset (magnetic declination). Once calibrated, the finder aims at true North.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_PLANET_DEF: Solar System body (Mercury to Neptune, plus the Moon, the Sun and Pluto). Their position changes hour by hour, unlike stars.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_STAR_DEF: Distant sun that shines by itself. Its celestial position (RA / Dec) is almost fixed; only azimuth and elevation change with time and place.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_GALAXY_DEF: Island of billions of stars (e.g. Andromeda, M51). Best seen away from cities, often with binoculars or a telescope.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SAT_DEF: Object orbiting Earth (ISS, Hubble, Landsat…). It moves quickly: azimuth and elevation are recomputed continuously.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ISS_DEF: International Space Station. It looks like a very bright point crossing the sky in a few minutes, without twinkling.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ZENITH_DEF: The point in the sky straight above your head (elevation 90°).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_NADIR_DEF: The point opposite the zenith, under your feet (elevation −90°). For a satellite, nadir is the ground point directly below it.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_CARD_DEF: North, East, South, West (and combinations: NE, SSW…). They summarize azimuth as a readable direction.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_OBS_DEF: Your position (GPS, address or map). All azimuth, elevation and visibility calculations start from this point.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SIGHT_DEF: Finder button: place the real object on the pointer (reticle), then tap. The app locks camera azimuth and elevation to that direction, to correct sensor error.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_POSE_DEF: Finder button: freezes the object in the picture. While paused, drag to pan in any direction and zoom — names grow. Tap again to resume tracking.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_TRAIL_DEF: Finder switch: draws the path the star or satellite will follow across the sky. Duration is set under Trajectory. Satellites: a few minutes (SGP4 orbit). Sky objects: longer (Earth’s rotation).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ASTERISM_DEF: A familiar star pattern that is not an official constellation: Big Dipper, Summer Triangle, Orion’s Belt, Sagittarius Teapot…
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ZODIAC_DEF: Sky band where the Sun, Moon and planets travel. The 12 zodiac constellations (plus Ophiuchus) lie along the ecliptic.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ECLIPTIC_DEF: The Sun’s yearly path, and Earth’s orbital plane. Planets stay close to this line in the sky.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_CELEQ_DEF: Earth’s equator projected onto the sky. Declination is 0° there. It meets the horizon due east and west, except at the poles.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SPHERE_DEF: Imaginary vault on which we place the stars. Right ascension and declination are coordinates on this sphere.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_MERIDIAN_DEF: The sky’s north–south semicircle through the zenith. A body is usually highest when it crosses this line.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LY_DEF: Distance light travels in one year (~9.46 trillion km). Sirius is 8.6 ly away; Andromeda about 2.5 million ly.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_PARSEC_DEF: Astronomers’ distance unit: 1 pc ≈ 3.26 light-years. Galaxies are often measured in megaparsecs (Mpc).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ABSMAG_DEF: How bright the object would be at 10 parsecs. It compares stars’ true output, unlike apparent magnitude (what you see).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SPECTRAL_DEF: Star class by temperature and colour: O B A F G K M (hottest/bluest to coolest/reddest). The Sun is G2.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_BINARY_DEF: Two or more stars bound by gravity. Albireo and Mizar–Alcor are famous pairs, sometimes split by eye or binoculars.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_VARIABLE_DEF: A star whose brightness changes (pulsation, eclipse, outburst). Algol, Mira and Delta Cephei are catalog examples.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_POLESTAR_DEF: A star near a celestial pole. North: Polaris (almost fixed). South: Sigma Octantis, much fainter.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_REDGIANT_DEF: An aged, swollen, orange star (Betelgeuse, Antares, Aldebaran). Very luminous even though cooler than the Sun.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SUPERNOVA_DEF: Explosion of a massive star at the end of its life. It can outshine a whole galaxy for weeks, then leave a remnant.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_MESSIER_DEF: 110 deep-sky objects (M1–M110) listed in the 18th century. M31 = Andromeda, M51 = Whirlpool, M42 = Orion Nebula.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_NGC_DEF: New General Catalogue (and Index Catalogue) numbers for nebulae, clusters and galaxies (NGC 224 = Andromeda, NGC 253 = Sculptor…).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LOCALGROUP_DEF: Our small galaxy family: Milky Way, Andromeda (M31), Triangulum (M33) and dozens of dwarfs (Magellanic Clouds, Draco Dwarf…).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LMC_DEF: Two dwarf galaxies orbiting the Milky Way, spectacular in the southern sky: Large (LMC) and Small (SMC) Magellanic Cloud.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_DEEPSKY_DEF: Objects beyond the Solar System other than single stars: galaxies, nebulae, clusters. Often too faint for the naked eye in cities.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_CLUSTER_DEF: Stars born together. Open cluster (Pleiades, Hyades): loose. Globular cluster: a ball of hundreds of thousands of stars.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_NEBULA_DEF: A cloud of gas and dust. Some are star nurseries (Orion); others are explosion leftovers (Crab / M1).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SPIRAL_DEF: Spiral (arms, like Andromeda), elliptical (a ball of old stars, M87) or irregular (Magellanic Clouds).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_QUASAR_DEF: Extremely bright core of a distant galaxy, powered by a supermassive black hole. Not naked-eye, but found in deep catalogues.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_TLE_DEF: A satellite’s orbit card. The finder uses it, via SGP4, to compute the current position of the ISS, Hubble, Sentinel…
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_NORAD_DEF: Unique ID of an orbiting object in the US catalogue (SATCAT). ISS = 25544, Hubble = 20580.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LEO_DEF: Typical altitude 200–2,000 km. ISS (~420 km) and Hubble (~540 km) fly there: a pass lasts only a few minutes.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_GEOORB_DEF: At ~35,786 km the satellite stays over one equatorial longitude (Astra 19.2°E, Hotbird, Meteosat). It does not cross the sky.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_L2_DEF: Sun–Earth balance region ~1.5 million km beyond Earth. James Webb, Euclid and Gaia observe there, away from Earth’s glare.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_INCL_DEF: Angle between the orbit and the equator. 0° = equatorial (GEO); ~98° = sun-synchronous polar (Sentinel, Landsat): covers the whole Earth.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_PERIOD_DEF: Time for one trip around Earth. ~92 min for the ISS, 24 h for a geostationary satellite.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_APOGEE_DEF: Farthest (apogee) and nearest (perigee) points from Earth on the orbit. Around the Sun: aphelion / perihelion.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SGP4_DEF: Model that turns a TLE into a satellite position at a given time. It powers ISS passes and the finder’s satellite chips.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_STARLINK_DEF: A line of newly launched Starlink satellites still bunched together. After dusk they look like a string of dots crossing the sky.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_OPPOSITION_DEF: The planet is opposite the Sun: it rises at sunset and stays up all night. Best time for Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_CONJUNCTION_DEF: The body lines up with the Sun (or another body). Mercury and Venus are often lost in the Sun’s glare then.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_RETRO_DEF: An illusion: a planet seems to back up among the stars when Earth overtakes it. Common for Mars.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_EQUINOX_DEF: When the Sun crosses the celestial equator (around 20 March and 22 September). Day and night are then about equal.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SOLSTICE_DEF: Sun at its highest (June) or lowest (December) declination. Longest / shortest day of the year.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SIDEREAL_DEF: Time tied to Earth’s spin relative to the stars, not the Sun. It tells which constellations are on the meridian.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_J2000_DEF: 1 January 2000 reference for catalogue RA/Dec. The finder uses these “fixed” positions for stars and galaxies.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LIGHTPOL_DEF: City glow that washes out faint objects. Galaxies and the Milky Way need a dark sky; the magnitude slider helps filter the lists.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_REFRACTION_DEF: Air bends light: near the horizon a body looks a bit higher than it is. Rise and set times allow for this.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ARCSEC_DEF: 1° = 60′ = 3,600″. The Moon and Sun are ~30′ wide. An arcsecond is tiny — for telescopes, not naked-eye aiming.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ANGULAR_DEF: How wide an object looks in the sky, in degrees. Andromeda spans ~3°, larger than the Moon, but its glow is very diffuse.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_COMET_DEF: A chunk of ice and dust. Near the Sun it grows a coma and tail. Rarely in fixed lists: the orbit is very stretched.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ASTEROID_DEF: A small rocky body, mostly between Mars and Jupiter. A few (Vesta) are binocular objects; most stay faint points.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_DWARF_DEF: Rounded enough to be spherical, but has not cleared its orbit. Pluto, Ceres, Eris. Pluto is listed among the finder’s planets.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_MAGFILTER_DEF: Finder slider: keep only stars brighter than a limit (default 6 ≈ naked eye). Raise it to show more faint stars.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_VISIBLEONLY_DEF: Option that hides targets below the horizon. Turn it off to browse the full catalogue (stars, galaxies, constellations, satellites).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_MILKYWAY_DEF: Our galaxy, seen from inside as a milky band. Spectacular under a dark sky; washed out in cities by light pollution.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_BAYER_DEF: A star named by a Greek letter and its constellation: α CMa = Sirius, β Ori = Rigel. α is usually the brightest.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_PARALLAX_DEF: Tiny yearly shift of a nearby star as Earth orbits the Sun. It underpins the parsec and Gaia distances.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_PROPERMOT_DEF: A star’s real drift across the sky, in milliarcseconds per year. For the finder, almost all stars stay “fixed” in a lifetime.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_TWINKLE_DEF: Stars flicker because of turbulent air. A planet or the ISS looks “wider” and twinkles far less — a clue to tell them apart.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_WHITEDWARF_DEF: The cooled core of a Sun-like star, extremely dense. Sirius B is one, far too faint for the naked eye next to Sirius.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_NEUTRON_DEF: Ultra-dense remnant of a supernova. A pulsar sweeps radio (sometimes light) beams around like a lighthouse.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_BLACKHOLE_DEF: An object whose gravity holds even light. M87 hosts a supermassive one; Sagittarius A* sits at the Milky Way’s centre.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_MAINSEQ_DEF: The hydrogen-burning phase (Sun, Vega, Sirius). Afterwards: red giant, then white dwarf or supernova, depending on mass.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_EXOPLANET_DEF: A planet around another star. TESS and Kepler find them via tiny eclipses. Too faint to aim at by eye.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_REDSHIFT_DEF: Light from distant galaxies stretches (z) as the Universe expands. Larger z means farther and younger-looking.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_VIRGO_DEF: The nearest big galaxy cluster, in Virgo and Coma: M87, M49, M84… The finder lists several under Galaxies.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_IAU_DEF: The International Astronomical Union fixed 88 constellations that cover the whole sky, with no gaps or overlaps.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_STICKFIG_DEF: Finder lines that join stars to sketch Orion, the Dipper, the Summer Triangle… A memory aid, not a physical link.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_MEO_DEF: Between LEO and GEO, around 20,000 km. GPS and Galileo fly there: slower than the ISS, never fixed like Astra.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SSO_DEF: A polar orbit (~98°) that crosses Earth at the same solar time. Sentinel, Landsat, NOAA: comparable photos day after day.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_FLARE_DEF: A flash when a panel or antenna reflects the Sun (old Iridiums, sometimes Starlink). Brighter than a star, then it fades.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SPACETEL_DEF: An observatory in orbit, above the atmosphere: Hubble (LEO), James Webb / Euclid / Gaia (L2), Chandra and XMM (high orbits).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_TIANGONG_DEF: China’s space station (CSS), a bit lower than the ISS. Aim it the same way: a bright, non-twinkling point for a few minutes.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ECLIPSE_DEF: Solar: the Moon covers the Sun. Lunar: Earth casts its shadow on the Moon. Needs a Sun–Earth–Moon line-up.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_OCCULT_DEF: A nearby body (often the Moon) passes in front of a star or planet and blanks it out. Used to measure positions and sizes.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_TWILIGHT_DEF: Civil (Sun 0° to −6°): still readable. Nautical (−6° to −12°). Astronomical (−12° to −18°): the sky is dark enough for faint stars.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SEEING_DEF: Air jitter that blurs views. Bad seeing makes stars dance; planets and the ISS look calmer.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_BORTLE_DEF: Sky quality from 1 (desert, blazing Milky Way) to 9 (city centre). At Bortle 8–9 only planets and the brightest stars remain.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_METEOR_DEF: The streak of a grain burning in the air (shooting star). Meteorite = what hits the ground. Fireball = a very bright meteor.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SHOWER_DEF: A swarm (Perseids, Geminids) when Earth crosses a comet’s trail. Streaks seem to radiate from a point in a constellation.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_AURORA_DEF: Glow (green, red) when the solar wind excites polar air. Borealis in the north, australis in the south. Rare at French latitudes except in a solar storm.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ZODLIGHT_DEF: A faint cone along the ecliptic after dusk, from Solar System dust. Only under a very dark sky.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ALBEDO_DEF: Fraction of sunlight bounced back. Venus is very bright thanks to high albedo (clouds); the Moon much less so.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_EARTHSHINE_DEF: The dark part of a crescent Moon stays visible, lit by Earth. Common a few days after (or before) new Moon.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LIBRATION_DEF: A slight lunar wobble that reveals a bit more than 50 % of the surface over weeks — never the whole far side.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SUPERMOON_DEF: Full Moon near perigee: a little larger and brighter than average. The difference to the eye is real but modest.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_GASGIANT_DEF: Jupiter and Saturn: mostly hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune: more ices. No solid surface to aim at.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_KUIPER_DEF: The region beyond Neptune (Pluto, trans-Neptunian objects). Too far for the finder, except Pluto already in the planet list.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_OORT_DEF: A spherical reservoir of comets at the edge of the Solar System. Long-period comets are thought to come from there.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_PRECESSION_DEF: Earth’s axis slowly sweeps in ~26,000 years: the pole star changes (Thuban once, Vega later). That is why catalogues use J2000.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_HOURANGLE_DEF: Sidereal time since the object crossed the meridian. 0 h = on the meridian (often culmination); positive = already west.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_FOV_DEF: How much sky the finder camera shows, in degrees. A wide field catches more objects; zoom tightens the reticle.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SURFBRIGHT_DEF: Glow per unit of sky angle. A spread-out galaxy (Andromeda) can have a decent total magnitude but a very diluted sheen — harder than a star of the same mag.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_AVERTED_DEF: Look slightly beside a faint object. Peripheral retina is more sensitive: galaxies and nebulae then “pop”.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_DARKADAPT_DEF: Eyes need 15–30 min to become sensitive. White light resets this; a red lamp preserves it.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_INFERIOR_DEF: Inferior (Mercury, Venus): orbits inside Earth’s, always near the Sun. Superior (Mars to Neptune): can be at opposition, all night.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_PLANNEB_DEF: Shell shed by a Sun-like star as it becomes a white dwarf (Lyra M57, Helix). Not a planet, despite the name.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_TERMINATOR_DEF: The day/night line on the Moon (or a planet). Relief is strongest there: best time for craters and mountains.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_UMBRA_DEF: Umbra: fully shadowed. Penumbra: partial dimming. A total lunar eclipse happens in Earth’s umbra.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_HR_DEF: Hertzsprung–Russell plot: temperature (spectral type) vs luminosity. It shows the main sequence, giants, and white dwarfs.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LUMCLASS_DEF: MK suffix: I = supergiant, III = giant, V = main-sequence dwarf. The Sun is G2V; Betelgeuse is M1–2Ia.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_TEFF_DEF: Black-body temperature that would radiate as much as the star (photosphere). Sun ≈ 5770 K; a red giant ~3500 K; an O star > 30,000 K.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_METAL_DEF: Abundance of elements heavier than H and He, written [Fe/H]. Population I (disk, like the Sun) is more “metal-rich” than Population II (halo, globulars).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_CHANDRA_DEF: Maximum mass of a white dwarf (~1.4 M☉). Beyond that, collapse yields a Type Ia supernova or a neutron star.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SCHWARZ_DEF: Event-horizon radius of a non-spinning black hole: Rs = 2GM/c². For the Sun it would be ~3 km; light cannot escape.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ACCRETION_DEF: Matter spiralling onto a compact object (black hole, neutron star). Friction heats the gas: X-rays, quasars, X-ray binaries.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_BROWNDWARF_DEF: Too light to fuse hydrogen (~13–80 Jupiter masses). Spectral types L, T, Y. Neither star nor planet: an in-between.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_WOLFRAYET_DEF: A very hot massive star (WR) that has shed its outer layers: fierce wind, broad emission lines, often a supernova progenitor.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_CEPHEID_DEF: A pulsating variable whose period sets its true luminosity. A standard candle for distances to nearby galaxies.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SNR_DEF: Shell and shock left after the blast (Crab M1, Cassiopeia A). Often bright in radio and X-rays, sometimes a binocular object.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_HII_DEF: Hydrogen ionised by young O/B stars. Orion (M42) is the prototype: red in Hα, a stellar nursery.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_EMNEB_DEF: Emission: the gas itself glows (ionised, Hα/OIII). Reflection: dust scatters nearby starlight (bluish, M78). Often mixed.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_DARKNEB_DEF: A dust cloud that blocks the starry background (Horsehead, Coal Sack, Barnard objects). Seen by silhouette, not by its own glow.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_AGN_DEF: A galactic core fed by a supermassive black hole that is accreting: Seyferts, quasars, blazars. Jet and disk dominate the light.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SEYFERT_DEF: A spiral with a very bright nucleus and broad (type 1) or narrow (type 2) spectral lines. M77 (NGC 1068) is a classic example.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LENSING_DEF: A mass (cluster, galaxy) bends light from a farther object: arcs, Einstein ring, multiple images. Microlensing can also reveal exoplanets.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_HUBBLELAW_DEF: Galaxies recede at v ≈ H0 × d. H0 (~70 km/s/Mpc) measures expansion. Cosmological redshift is the signature.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_CMB_DEF: Fossil light from the Big Bang, now 2.7 K microwaves. The oldest light we can see, from before galaxies formed.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_DARKMATTER_DEF: Mass that emits no light, inferred from rotation curves and lensing. It dominates galaxy halos, including the Milky Way’s.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_DARKENERGY_DEF: The component that accelerates cosmic expansion (cosmological constant Λ). Not a finder target: a purely cosmological effect.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ICRS_DEF: International Celestial Reference System: a quasi-inertial frame based on quasars, realised by Gaia. J2000/FK5 is a practical approximation.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_GALCOORD_DEF: Longitude ℓ and latitude b relative to the Milky Way plane (ℓ = 0° toward the centre, Sagittarius). Complements equatorial RA/Dec.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ECLCOORD_DEF: Longitude λ and latitude β in Earth’s orbital plane. Natural for the Solar System: planets stay near β ≈ 0°.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_OBLIQUITY_DEF: Tilt of Earth’s axis to the ecliptic, ≈ 23.4°. It causes the seasons and the gap between celestial equator and ecliptic.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_NUTATION_DEF: A short wobble (~18.6 yr, from the Moon) of Earth’s axis, on top of precession. Precision catalogues (ICRS) correct for it.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ABERRATION_DEF: An apparent shift (~20″ yearly) because Earth moves while light is arriving. Distinct from parallax, which depends on distance.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_TOPOCENTRIC_DEF: Geocentric: from Earth’s centre. Topocentric: from your site. For the Moon and satellites the azimuth/elevation difference is obvious.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_JULIAN_DEF: A continuous day count from −4712. MJD = JD − 2,400,000.5. Ephemerides and TLE epochs use this, not the civil calendar.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LST_DEF: Hour angle of the vernal point at your meridian. When LST equals an object’s RA, it transits. The sky’s clock, not the Sun’s.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_KEPLER_DEF: 1) elliptical orbits, Sun at one focus. 2) equal areas in equal times (faster at perihelion). 3) P² ∝ a³: period tied to the semi-major axis.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SMA_DEF: The ellipse parameter a: the orbit’s “mean radius”. For Earth, a = 1 AU. Kepler’s third law links a to the period.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ECC_DEF: How stretched the ellipse is: e = 0 circle, e near 1 a long orbit (comets). e ≥ 1: parabola or hyperbola (unbound objects).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ANOMALY_DEF: The angle that locates a body on its orbit. True: from periapsis, geometric. Mean: proportional to time, used in TLEs.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_RAAN_DEF: Right ascension of the ascending node: where the orbit crosses the equator northbound. With argument of periapsis, it orients the ellipse.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SYNODIC_DEF: Time between two identical configurations as seen from Earth (two full Moons, two Mars oppositions). Longer than the sidereal period.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_QUADRATURE_DEF: Elongation of 90°: the planet stands east or west of the Sun. For Mars, a good time to see the terminator.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ROCHE_DEF: Distance inside which a satellite is torn apart by tides. Saturn’s rings lie near this limit.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_HILL_DEF: The volume where a body’s gravity beats the Sun’s (or the planet’s). The Moon stays inside Earth’s Hill sphere; beyond it, no stable moon.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_TIDALLOCK_DEF: Rotation equal to revolution: the same face always toward the primary. Moon–Earth, Pluto–Charon, many of Jupiter’s moons.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LAGRANGE_DEF: Five equilibria in a two-body system. L1, L2, L3 in line; L4/L5 (Trojans) stable. JWST, Euclid, Gaia sit at Sun–Earth L2.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_AIRMASS_DEF: How much atmosphere the light crosses: 1 at the zenith, ~2 at 30° elevation, much more near the horizon. Higher airmass means fainter, redder objects.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_EXTINCTION_DEF: Dimming of light. Atmospheric: depends on airmass. Interstellar (AV, reddening): galactic dust, strongest near the plane.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_COLORINDEX_DEF: Difference of blue and visual magnitudes. Small B−V = hot/blue star; large B−V = cool/red. Basis of UBV photometry.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_POGSON_DEF: One magnitude = a flux factor of 2.512 (⁵√100). Five magnitudes = ×100. Hence negative mag for very bright objects (Sun −26.7).
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_NELM_DEF: Faintest star still visible, typically 6 under a good sky, 2–3 in a city. Tied to Bortle and the finder’s magnitude slider.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ZHR_DEF: Meteors per hour an ideal observer would see with the radiant at the zenith and a perfect sky. Perseids peak around 100.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_AIRY_DEF: The diffraction spot of a star at a telescope focus. Its diameter θ ≈ 1.22 λ/D sets the instrument’s theoretical resolution.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_RAYLEIGH_DEF: Two stars are resolvable if one peak sits on the other’s first minimum (~140″/Dmm). Dawes’ limit is a little tighter.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_EXITPUPIL_DEF: Diameter of the beam leaving the eyepiece (D/G). Beyond ~7 mm the eye cannot use it; too small, the image is dim.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_FOCALRATIO_DEF: Focal length / aperture. f/4 = fast, wide field (deep sky). f/10 = more contrast, easier on Moon and planets.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_FILTERS_DEF: Narrowband filters that isolate emission-nebula lines. OIII and UHC help visually; Hα is mainly for imaging.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_HEO_DEF: A highly elliptical High Earth Orbit: long dwell near apogee over one region (Russian Molniya). Hubble is not this: it is in LEO.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_MEANMOTION_DEF: Revolutions per day in a TLE (ISS ≈ 15.5). n = 86400/P. The inverse of the period, used by SGP4.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_BSTAR_DEF: Atmospheric-drag term in a TLE. Larger (in LEO) means the satellite slows and decays. SGP4 uses it to propagate the orbit.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_KESSLER_DEF: A cascade of debris collisions in orbit: each impact creates more fragments. Worst in LEO, hence NORAD catalogue tracking.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_GROUNDTRACK_DEF: The satellite’s nadir projected on Earth. For the ISS, a sine wave that drifts west each revolution.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_HOHMANN_DEF: The minimum-Δv elliptical burn to go from one circular orbit to another. Trips to Mars or GEO often follow this idea.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_PHOTOSPHERE_DEF: Photosphere: the Sun’s visible surface (~5800 K). Chromosphere: pink Hα layer. Corona: tenuous halo, millions of K, seen in a total eclipse.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_SOLARWIND_DEF: Plasma (protons, electrons) blown out by the Sun, carving the heliosphere. It warps magnetospheres and feeds auroras.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_CME_DEF: A plasma blob torn from the corona. If it hits Earth: geomagnetic storm, low-latitude auroras, sometimes radio blackouts.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_MAGNETOSPHERE_DEF: The planet’s magnetic cavity in the solar wind. Around Earth: Van Allen belts. Jupiter’s is enormous.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_TROJAN_DEF: Asteroids (or moons) stable at a planet’s L4 and L5, 60° ahead and behind. Jupiter has thousands; Earth has a few.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_NEO_DEF: An asteroid or comet whose orbit comes near Earth. PHAs (potentially hazardous) are watched closely.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_LIGHTTIME_DEF: How long light takes to reach us. Moon ~1.3 s, Sun ~8 min, Jupiter 30–50 min. The finder often shows this with the distance.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_STDCANDLE_DEF: An object of known intrinsic brightness (Cepheids, Type Ia supernovae). Measure the received flux, infer the distance.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_ROTCURVE_DEF: Stellar speed vs distance from the centre. It stays flat instead of falling: a main argument for dark matter in the halo.
ASTRO_COMPASS.HELP_OSCULATING_DEF: The Keplerian ellipse tangent to the real orbit at instant T (epoch). TLEs are not that: they are mean elements fitted for SGP4.
ASTRO_COMPASS.OBJECT_INFO_OPEN_HINT: All details about the selected object
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_OPEN_HINT: Step-by-step: aim, align, and finder tools
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_INTRO: Point the back of the phone at the sky. The selected object appears in the image as soon as it enters the field of view, and turns green when it is on the reticle.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_START_HINT: Tap “Enable sensors and camera”. On iPhone this tap is required. Also allow GPS: every calculation starts from your location.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_TARGET_HINT: Pick a planet, star, galaxy, satellite (ISS, Astra 19.2°E, Starlink train…) or a custom object (RA / Dec). The last target is remembered. “Visible targets only” hides objects below the horizon. Or start live auto-detect.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_AIM_HINT: Hold the phone upright, rear camera toward the sky. Turn until the object enters the image. Camera numbers follow the phone; Target stays on the object’s direction.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_GUIDE_HINT: Chevrons show how to turn: left / right for azimuth, up / down for elevation. A check mark appears when the aim is good.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_LOCK_HINT: When the object sits on the reticle, the finder turns green. That is the moment to observe, align position, or tap Pause.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_CUE_HINT: Choose Off, Beep or Vibrate. The cue fires when the object is centered, so you can aim without watching the screen.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_NORTH_HINT: Phone flat, top toward geographic North, then tap. Or top toward South and “This is South”: North is aligned as N = S − 180°. “Reset to 0” clears it.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_SIGHT_HINT: Place the real object (e.g. Venus) on the reticle, then tap. The app offsets azimuth and elevation so the overlay matches the sky.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_CAL_HINT: “North calibration” opens the Direction page: figure-8, GPS walk, Sun, then 7 camera poses (N, W, S, E, 45° sky, zenith, ground) to also calibrate elevation.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_PAUSE_HINT: Freezes the object and the camera image. Zoom also works without pause. While paused, drag to pan the view (including fullscreen) and zoom. Tap again to resume tracking.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_TRAIL_HINT: Draws the future path in the finder, with minute marks. Duration is set under Trajectory.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_ZOOM_HINT: Pinch, mouse wheel or buttons (1× to 8×). While paused, drag to pan the view. Object names grow with zoom. Tap the factor to return to 1×.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_FS_HINT: Enlarges the finder. While paused, zoom and pan stay available, along with cues and this how-to.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_AUTO_HINT: Continuously tracks the object you are pointing at. Filter planets, stars, galaxies and satellites. “Naked eye” and “Max magnitude” keep only bright enough objects. Pause freezes detection; zoom and fullscreen work in this view too. “Keep in finder” (off by default) keeps the identified object as the finder target when you leave.
ASTRO_COMPASS.FINDER_INFO_FICHE_HINT: The Object (i) button shows type, magnitudes, distances, visibility, the constellation stick figure (enlargeable in the slideshow) and a Wikipedia link.

NORD.TITLE: Compass
NORD.SUBTITLE: North compass from the magnetic sensor, plus a live readout of the phone sensors (same as the *#0*# diagnostic screen).
NORD.PERMISSION_NEEDED: iOS needs a tap: use the button to allow compass and motion access.
NORD.PERMISSION_DENIED: Sensor access denied. Allow it in Settings, then try again.
NORD.TRUE_NORTH_UNAVAILABLE: GPS required: without a location fix, true north is off (magnetic heading).
NORD.DECLINATION_HINT: Magnetic → true north (GPS). Changes only if you travel far.
NORD.ADDRESS_EMPTY: No address yet — enable GPS or tap refresh.
NORD.FIELD_INTERFERENCE: Unusual field (outside 22–72 µT): move away from magnets, speakers and magnetic cases.
NORD.CAL_INTRO: The magnetometer drifts near metal. A figure-8 measures hard-iron bias, then the gyro locks heading — that is what keeps it stable.
NORD.CAL_FIGURE8_HINT: Draw a figure-8 in the air, rotating the phone on every axis, away from metal.
NORD.CAL_SETTLE_HINT: Hold the phone still and flat…
NORD.CAL_DONE: North locked. The gyro holds heading; the magnetometer only corrects very slowly.
NORD.SENSORS_HINT: Extra web APIs. Green = live. Dimmed = API missing on this device.
NORD.SENSORS_HW_HINT: The six sensors from the Samsung screen: accelerometer, barometer, proximity/light, gyroscope, magnetic sensor (compass) and fingerprint.
NORD.NORTH_FROM_MAG: North is read from the magnetic sensor.
NORD.S_MAG_NOTE: This is the same sensor as “Magnetic Sensor” in *#0*#. The x, y, z (µT) values and azimuth are used to find North.
NORD.S_MAG_NOTE_OS: The browser may not expose raw x/y/z, but azimuth still comes from the same magnetic sensor (OS fusion).
NORD.S_BARO_NOTE: hPa pressure is almost never exposed to the web. GPS altitude is shown when GPS is on.
NORD.S_PROXY_LIGHT_NOTE: Same “PROXY & LIGHT” block as the diagnostic. Browsers often allow light, not proximity.
NORD.S_FINGER_NOTE: The *#0*# NORMALSCAN / SENSORINFO test cannot be run from a website.
NORD.S_OIS_NOTE: The OIS gyro (optical image stabilization) is not exposed to the browser.

DIRECTION.TITLE: Calibration
DIRECTION.TARGET_HELP: A ground landmark replaces North. Pin it on the map, aim at it, save. You can later change the name, photo or landmark, then save. The i button shows the diagram.
DIRECTION.HOLD_VERTICAL: Hold the phone upright (portrait), screen toward you — not flat.
DIRECTION.HOLD_FLAT: Hold the phone flat, screen to the sky, top toward North.
DIRECTION.TARGET_MARK_HINT: Double-click the landmark in Trace Viewer, close, then aim at it upright from wherever you are to lock.
DIRECTION.TARGET_MARK_NEAR: Landmark too close ({{m}} m): GPS is inaccurate. Prefer a distant object.
DIRECTION.TARGET_NEED_SENSORS: Enable the sensors to aim at the target.
DIRECTION.TARGET_PHOTO_EMPTY: No photo yet — aim at the target, then take one.
DIRECTION.TARGET_PHOTO_NEED_CAM: Start the camera to take a photo.
DIRECTION.TARGET_EDIT_HELP: Move the markers, change the name or photo, then save.
DIRECTION.TARGET_EDIT_MAP_HINT: Drag the blue pin (you) and the red pin (target), or tap the map to place the active point.
DIRECTION.TARGET_EDIT_NEED_GPS: Current GPS is not available yet.
DIRECTION.TARGET_UPDATE_HINT: Saves the name, photo, your position and the landmark, without recalibrating heading.
DIRECTION.TARGET_CHECK_HINT: Aim at the target, then compare GPS and heading with the last lock.
DIRECTION.TARGET_CHECK_OK: Nothing moved: GPS and heading are stable. No need to recalibrate.
DIRECTION.TARGET_CHECK_NEED: Aim at the target first (sensors on), then run the check again.
DIRECTION.TARGET_CHECK_GPS: You moved about {{m}} m from the saved point.
DIRECTION.TARGET_CHECK_HEAD: Heading on the target drifted by {{deg}}° since the last lock.
DIRECTION.TARGET_CHECK_ADVICE: Recalibrate this target now, or the sky finder will be off.
DIRECTION.TARGET_LIST_EMPTY: No target saved for this account.
DIRECTION.TARGET_DELETE_CONFIRM: Delete this target and its photo?
DIRECTION.TARGET_SAVE_FAIL: Could not save. Sign in, then try again.
DIRECTION.SUBTITLE: Phone flat, top toward North, tap Save, then calibrate the finder if needed.
DIRECTION.QUICK_HINT: Phone flat, top toward North, then tap. The magnetometer is more reliable that way. The number is the heading correction — the same as in the sky finder.
DIRECTION.INFO_OPEN_HINT: How North lock works (and why it drifts)
DIRECTION.INFO_OPEN_HINT_CIBLE: How to lock a landmark from anywhere
DIRECTION.INFO_NORTH_LEAD: North tells the phone which way it is pointing.
DIRECTION.INFO_NORTH_P1: Phone flat, top toward true north — or figure-8, a GPS walk, or the Sun. Flat is better for the magnetometer. The number is the correction. It is the same one used in the sky finder.
DIRECTION.INFO_NORTH_P2: You do not have to use North: the Target tab replaces it with a fixed object (tower, antenna, summit).
DIRECTION.INFO_NORTH_DRIFT: Watch out: the phone sensor drifts, especially near metal. After a few minutes the finder can be wrong. Recalibrate North, or aim at your target again.
DIRECTION.INFO_CIBLE_LEAD: A target is an object you can see. It replaces North.
DIRECTION.INFO_CIBLE_P1: 1) Pin the landmark on the map (its GPS). 2) Phone upright, aim the camera at that object. 3) Save. The app then knows: “I am looking toward the tower.”
DIRECTION.INFO_CIBLE_ANYWHERE: Why from anywhere? The app knows the tower GPS and yours. It computes the current you → tower angle. Aim at the object, not at the old degree number.
DIRECTION.INFO_CIBLE_DRIFT: This does not freeze phone drift. Five minutes later, if software north has moved: aim at the same tower and lock again. No need to find North.
DIRECTION.INFO_CIBLE_DIST: Pick a distant landmark (hundreds of metres, or kilometres). Too close (under 80 m), GPS azimuth is unreliable.
DIRECTION.INFO_SCHEMA_CAPTION: Same tower, new place: the angle changes (40° then 70°). That is expected. Aim at the tower — the app recomputes it.
DIRECTION.STEP_OTHER_HELP: If aiming at North is impractical: figure-8, GPS walk, or Sun. They change the same number.
DIRECTION.STEP_VISOR_HELP: 7 camera poses also calibrate up/down (elevation). Useful for the sky finder.
DIRECTION.NEED_TAP: iOS requires a tap to allow motion sensors.
DIRECTION.CAM_RESIZE_HINT: Drag to change the height. Double-click to reset.
DIRECTION.CAM_PLACEHOLDER: Rear camera — point the back of the phone at the landscape.
DIRECTION.TRUE_NORTH_UNAVAILABLE: GPS required: without a location fix, true north is off (magnetic heading).
DIRECTION.ROSE_ARIA: Compass rose, camera aiming at the top mark
DIRECTION.CAL_HINT: Figure-8 in the air to calibrate the magnetometer.
DIRECTION.CAL_MOVE: Keep rotating the phone on every axis
DIRECTION.CAL_NORTH_HELP: These methods only correct heading (azimuth). The sky viewfinder also needs elevation — see below.
DIRECTION.CAL_METHOD_AUTO_HINT: Trace a figure-8 in the air to calibrate the magnetometer.
DIRECTION.CAL_METHOD_MANUAL_HINT: Phone flat, top toward North, then save.
DIRECTION.CAL_METHOD_GPS_HINT: Walk straight ahead: GPS aligns North.
DIRECTION.CAL_METHOD_SUN_HINT: Point the camera at the Sun (daytime).
DIRECTION.CAL_MANUAL_STEP1: Stay away from metal and magnets.
DIRECTION.CAL_MANUAL_STEP2: Phone flat, screen to the sky: point the top toward North (true north if that toggle is on).
DIRECTION.CAL_MANUAL_STEP3: When the camera aims North, tap This is North.
DIRECTION.CAL_GPS_STEP1: Hold the phone as if aiming (camera forward).
DIRECTION.CAL_GPS_STEP3: GPS course of the walk aligns North.
DIRECTION.CAL_SUN_STEP1: Make sure the Sun is visible.
DIRECTION.CAL_SUN_STEP2: Point the rear camera straight at the Sun.
DIRECTION.CAL_SUN_STEP3: Tap Save: solar azimuth sets North.
DIRECTION.CAL_SUN_NIGHT: Sun below the horizon — method unavailable.
DIRECTION.FIG8_INTRO_MAG: The magnetic sensor was calibrated (hard-iron bias). The North correction was updated to follow the new heading.
DIRECTION.FIG8_INTRO_OS: The figure-8 covered the orientations. Without raw x/y/z, OS heading was used and the North correction was adjusted.
DIRECTION.FIG8_OFFSET_HINT: The North correction number is the same as in the sky finder. You can still adjust it by hand.
DIRECTION.UNAVAILABLE_ARIA: Sensors missing or denied on this device
DIRECTION.PAT_FORGET_CONFIRM: Delete all sensor poses for this account? The viewfinder will no longer be calibrated.
DIRECTION.PAT_FORGET_HINT: Deletes all poses. The viewfinder becomes uncalibrated.
DIRECTION.PAT_START_HINT: Walks through 7 aims (North, West, South, East, 45°, zenith, ground) so the viewfinder learns azimuth and elevation.
DIRECTION.PAT_EXPORT_HINT: Downloads a JSON file of the poses, to keep or reload later.
DIRECTION.PAT_IMPORT_HINT: Applies a JSON you saved earlier, without repeating the poses.
DIRECTION.PAT_VISOR_HELP: For the sky viewfinder: a series of 7 camera poses. Save keeps the file, Load reapplies it, Clear resets.
DIRECTION.PAT_MIX_LATEST_HINT: The viewfinder uses only the most recent series.
DIRECTION.PAT_MIX_AVG_HINT: The viewfinder averages the {{n}} series (steadier, a bit less reactive to a new capture).
DIRECTION.PAT_UNCAL: No poses in the database yet.
DIRECTION.PAT_IMPORT_FAIL: Pose file unreadable or incomplete (need at least 4 poses).
DIRECTION.PAT_MIX: {{n}} series — which one should the viewfinder use?
DIRECTION.PAT_EMPTY: No poses in the database for this account. Record on the phone (same user), then export here.
DIRECTION.PAT_SYNC_FAIL: Could not reach the database. Sign in, then try again.
DIRECTION.PAT_INTRO: At each step: aim the rear camera as shown, then Save. The four cardinal poses, 45° toward the sky, zenith and ground are used to compute look azimuth, elevation and roll.
DIRECTION.PAT_HOW: First set North by hand (camera toward North, horizon). Then 7 poses: N, W, S, E, 45° sky, zenith, ground. Completing the series calibrates the viewfinder — no code change. You can also import a previously exported JSON.
DIRECTION.PAT_FAIL: Not enough sensor data. Enable sensors, then start again.
DIRECTION.PAT_POSE_MISMATCH: The aim does not match this pose. Reposition the phone, then try again.
DIRECTION.PAT_POSE_NOT_SKY: The camera is not pointing at the zenith. Tilt until it aims straight overhead.
DIRECTION.PAT_POSE_NOT_GROUND: The camera is still pointing at the sky. For the ground: screen toward the sky, rear camera toward your feet.
DIRECTION.PAT_EXPECT_EL: Target: elevation {{el}}° (keep the same heading, change tilt only)
DIRECTION.PAT_NOT_ALIGNED: Not aligned yet — follow the instruction below
DIRECTION.PAT_COACH_SENSORS: First tap “Enable sensors and camera” at the top of the page.
DIRECTION.PAT_COACH_NORTH: Point the rear camera North, phone upright, horizon. When the heading shows about 0° N, tap “This is North”.
DIRECTION.PAT_COACH_ALIGN: Phone upright, portrait, screen toward you. Aim at the horizon. Turn until azimuth is close to the target.
DIRECTION.PAT_COACH_ALIGN_TILT: Do not turn (same azimuth). Slowly tilt the top of the phone backward until elevation ≈ +45°.
DIRECTION.PAT_COACH_ALIGN_SKY: Keep tilting slowly backward until elevation ≈ +90° (zenith). Hold still 1 s even if the readout jumps.
DIRECTION.PAT_COACH_ALIGN_GROUND: Point the rear camera straight at the ground, under your feet, until elevation ≈ −90°.
DIRECTION.PAT_COACH_SAVE: Good. Hold still and tap Save.
DIRECTION.PAT_DONE: Series saved. The viewfinder uses these poses (azimuth, gravity, offset). Export the JSON to keep it, or import one later.
DIRECTION.PAT_NORTH_HINT: Phone upright, aim at the horizon. Point the rear camera toward geographic North (true North if the True North box is checked).
DIRECTION.PAT_N_HINT: Phone upright (portrait), screen toward you. Aim at the horizon — not the ground or sky. Rear camera straight at geographic North.
DIRECTION.PAT_W_HINT: Keep the same tilt (still the horizon), turn 90° left. Rear camera West.
DIRECTION.PAT_S_HINT: Another 90° left, still the horizon. Rear camera South.
DIRECTION.PAT_E_HINT: Another 90° left, still the horizon. Rear camera East.
DIRECTION.PAT_TILT_HINT: Keep the same heading. From the horizon, slowly tilt the top of the phone backward until you aim ~45° above the horizon (halfway to zenith). This is where the object crosses below the reticle.
DIRECTION.PAT_SKY_HINT: Keep tilting slowly until the rear camera points straight at the zenith (overhead, +90°). Hold still 1 second, then Save — even if the numbers jump.
DIRECTION.PAT_GROUND_HINT: Point the rear camera straight at the ground, under your feet (−90°).
